lead: A context-free grammar can nest structures, but it cannot keep three independent counts equal. The pumping lemma turns that limit into a test: every long string in a context-free language has two small pieces that can be repeated together. It is used to prove that a language is not context-free, especially when studying the limits of parsers. It is a one-way test: failing it proves non-context-freeness, but passing it proves nothing.
prereq: You need: 3.2 for parse trees and 3.5 for CNF in the proof of the pumping length.

blocks.text: For every context-free language L there is a pumping length p ≥ 1 with this property. Every string s in L with |s| ≥ p can be split as s = uvwxy so that three conditions hold. Here u, v, w, x, y are strings over the same alphabet as L, i is a non-negative integer, and |z| means the length of z.
s = uvwxy with (1) |vwx| ≤ p, (2) |vx| ≥ 1, (3) uvⁱwxⁱy ∈ L for every i ≥ 0
blocks.where: p is the pumping length; u, v, w, x, y are the five pieces; i is the number of copies of v and x; |vwx| is the length of the middle block; |vx| is the total length of the two pumped pieces.

blocks.text: Condition (1) says the middle block vwx is short. Condition (2) says at least one of v and x is nonempty. Condition (3) says v and x are repeated together: i = 0 deletes both, i = 2 duplicates both. This is weaker than the regular-language pumping lemma, which pumps one piece. The lemma is one-way: it can prove that L is not context-free, but it cannot prove that L is context-free. Many non-context-free languages also satisfy it.

sections.h3: Why a long string repeats a variable

blocks.text: Take a grammar for L − {ε} in Chomsky normal form (CNF), with b variables; handle ε separately, since CNF rules cannot derive it. CNF rules have the form A → BC or A → a (see 3.5). Let q = 2^b and set the pumping length p = max(q, 1). A parse tree for a nonempty string s has variables at internal nodes and terminals at the leaves (see 3.2). If |s| ≥ p, the tree is tall enough that some root-to-leaf path contains the same variable twice. Call the upper occurrence A and the lower occurrence A.

Picture the upper A. Its yield is v w x: the lower A gives w, and the pieces around it give v and x. The rest of the tree gives u on the left and y on the right, so s = u v w x y. Because the lower A can replace the upper A, i = 0 gives u w y ∈ L. Because the upper A's rule can wrap the lower A again, i = 2 gives u v v w x x y ∈ L, and in general the upper A becomes vⁱ (lower A) xⁱ. The two occurrences are distinct, so at least one of v, x is nonempty, giving |vx| ≥ 1. Choose the repeated pair so that the upper A's subtree is short; with b variables this gives |vwx| ≤ q ≤ p.

items: Assume L is context-free and let p be its pumping length from the lemma.
Choose one string s ∈ L with |s| ≥ p. The string usually depends on p, such as aᵖbᵖcᵖ.
Write s = uvwxy and use |vwx| ≤ p and |vx| ≥ 1 to list the possible places where v and x can lie.
Pick i = 0 or i = 2, and show that uvⁱwxⁱy is not in L. One counterexample i is enough.
Conclude that the assumption was false, so L is not context-free.

blocks.text: For L = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 1}, the string s = aᵖbᵖcᵖ has length 3p. Since |vwx| ≤ p, the block vwx cannot touch all three letter blocks: touching a and c would require all p b's plus at least one a and one c. So some letter keeps count p while pumping changes another count. The same style of argument proves that {ww | w ∈ {a, b}*} is not context-free.

figure.caption: In s = a⁵b⁵c⁵ the window vwx holds at most 5 symbols, but reaching from the last a to the first c takes 7, so every window misses one block. Pumping with i = 2 grows the other counts while that block stays at 5, and the string leaves L.

examples.question: Use the pumping lemma for context-free languages to show L = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 1} is not context-free. For the calculation take p = 5 and s = a⁵b⁵c⁵. State |s|, the bound on |vwx|, the lower bound on |vx|, and explain what uv²wx²y looks like.
steps: Assume L is context-free. Let p be its pumping length. For this run set p = 5. The same argument works for every p.
Choose s = a⁵b⁵c⁵. The length is |s| = 5 + 5 + 5 = 15. Since 15 ≥ 5, s is long enough.
The lemma gives s = uvwxy with |vwx| ≤ 5, |vx| ≥ 1, and uv²wx²y ∈ L.
The block vwx has length at most 5. To touch a and c, vwx would need at least one a, all 5 b's, and one c, which is length at least 7. So vwx misses at least one letter block entirely.
Suppose the untouched block is c. Its count in uv²wx²y stays 5.
Pumping with i = 2 replaces v by vv and x by xx. Since |vx| ≥ 1, at least one symbol is added to a or b. So at least one of those counts becomes more than 5.
The three counts cannot all be 5, so uv²wx²y ∉ L. This contradicts the lemma. Therefore L is not context-free.

The other two cases are symmetric: if a is untouched its count stays 5 while b or c grows, and if b is untouched its count stays 5 while a or c grows. In every case the three counts cannot stay equal.
examples.answer: No split satisfies pumping with i = 2, so L is not context-free; with p = 5, |s| = 15, |vwx| ≤ 5, and |vx| ≥ 1.

s_len = 3 * p
max_vwx = p
min_vx = 1

print(max_vwx)
print(min_vx)
print(i)

traps: Using |vx| ≤ p instead of |vwx| ≤ p. v and x may sit far apart inside vwx; it is the whole block vwx that must be short.
Choosing v = x = ε. This breaks |vx| ≥ 1, and pumping with i = 0 or i = 2 changes nothing.
Checking only i = 0 and never i = 2, or the reverse. Pick the value of i that breaks the language.
Claiming a language is context-free because it passes the pumping lemma. The lemma is necessary, not sufficient.
Pumping v and x with different exponents. The lemma pumps both with the same i.

quiz.q: State the three conditions of the pumping lemma for context-free languages.
quiz.a: For some p ≥ 1, every s ∈ L with |s| ≥ p can be written s = uvwxy with |vwx| ≤ p, |vx| ≥ 1, and uvⁱwxⁱy ∈ L for every i ≥ 0.

quiz.q: Why are v and x pumped with the same i instead of separately?
quiz.a: They come from the two sides of the same repeated variable. Replacing the upper A by vⁱ (lower A) xⁱ inserts i copies of both pieces in one step, so the exponent must be the same.

quiz.q: For L = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}, take p = 4 and s = a⁴b⁴c⁴. Explain why vwx cannot contain at least one a, one b and one c.
quiz.a: To contain an a, a b and a c, vwx must include all 4 b's plus at least one a and one c. Its length would be at least 1 + 4 + 1 = 6, but |vwx| ≤ 4. So vwx misses at least one letter block.

quiz.q: A language passes the pumping lemma for context-free languages. Can you conclude that it is context-free? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The lemma is one-way. It says every context-free language has the pumping property, but some languages that are not context-free also have it. Passing is necessary but not sufficient.

quiz.q: In a pumping split s = uvwxy, can v be empty? Can x be empty? What is forbidden?
quiz.a: One of v and x may be empty, but both cannot be empty. The condition |vx| ≥ 1 forbids v = x = ε.

quiz.q: In the CNF proof, what is the pumping length p in terms of the number b of variables?
Why is the context-free pumping lemma weaker than the regular-language pumping lemma?
quiz.a: Both lemmas are one-way: passing proves nothing, failing proves non-membership. The context-free version is harder to apply because the split has five pieces, the two pumped pieces v and x are tied to one exponent i, and the only length bound is on the whole middle block (|vwx| ≤ p), not on v and x separately.

beyond: Not for the exam. Ogden's lemma strengthens this pumping lemma by letting you mark positions that must be pumped, which proves more languages non-context-free. Parikh's theorem gives a separate counting test for context-free languages. In research, pumping-style arguments are used in grammar inference and in proving limits of parser generators. Search next for Ogden's lemma and Parikh's theorem.
